title: 'Never Alter or Backdate': The H-1B Document Warning From an Immigration Lawyer
excerpt: Consulates are asking some long-pending H-1B applicants in India for fresh employment verification letters and social media details. A lawyer's guidance: answer truthfully, keep the email trail, and never submit a letter that claims a job exists when it does not.
body:
• US consular posts have in recent months asked some H-1B applicants in long-pending administrative processing for a recently dated employment verification letter, and for social media details, when requesting passports for final adjudication.
  • Immigration lawyer Gnanamookan Senthurjothi's core warning: do not misrepresent anything at this stage — it can jeopardize all future US immigration options.
  • If the job is no longer available, the lawful move is to take legal advice and answer truthfully — never to submit a letter claiming it still exists.
  • Willful, material misrepresentation to obtain a visa can trigger inadmissibility under INA section 212(a)(6)(C)(i); a request for updated verification is not, by itself, a fraud finding.

For H-1B applicants whose cases have sat in administrative processing for months, the final request from a consulate can look routine: send the passport, and send a fresh letter confirming the job is still there. Immigration lawyer Gnanamookan Senthurjothi is warning applicants in India not to treat that request casually, according to reporting of his guidance — because the temptation to tidy up the paperwork is exactly what can end a US career.

What consulates are asking for

Over the last few months, consular posts have sought recently dated employment verification letters from some applicants, confirming the job remains genuine and available, while also requesting passports for final adjudication. Social media profiles are also being asked for; disclosure has been mandatory for H-1B applicants since last December. None of that, Senthurjothi stresses, means the consulate has already decided anything adverse: a request for updated verification does not itself indicate a fraud finding.

"Willful, material misrepresentation to obtain a U.S. visa can trigger inadmissibility under INA § 212(a)(6)(C)(i), with potentially serious long-term consequences."

— Guidance cited by immigration lawyer Gnanamookan Senthurjothi

The rules that matter

The letter must come from an authorized HR representative or company official, be recently dated, and accurately confirm employment status and job availability. If the letter is attached to an email, keep the original email and include a printout when submitting, where appropriate. Documents must never be altered or backdated, and verification must not come from an unauthorized person. Requested documents and social media links should go through the designated channel, with links accurate and accessible.

If the job no longer exists

This is the trap the warning is really about. Long processing times mean some applicants' roles have been eliminated, restructured or withdrawn by the time the consulate writes. Senthurjothi's advice is blunt: you may seek legal advice before responding, but you should never submit a letter falsely claiming the job is still available. A truthful answer may end that particular visa application; a false one can trigger a permanent inadmissibility finding that follows the applicant across every future US visa category.

Why it matters now

The guidance lands in a year of intensified H-1B scrutiny — site visits, social media vetting and litigation over new fees — in which the documentary record an applicant creates is increasingly the case. For applicants in India waiting on stamping, the actionable step is simple: prepare the employer letter early, from the right signatory, with the email trail preserved, and let the facts be whatever they are.
